passages.happening:
“The end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land” (verse 2). God will judge the people by their ways and repay them for their abominations; he will not pity or spare them (verses 3-4). The poem repeats itself like a drumbeat: “The end has come! The end has come!” (verse 6). ‘The time has come; the day is near’ (verse 7).

“Behold, the day is here!” (verse 10). Violence has grown into a rod to punish wickedness (verse 11). ‘Let the buyer not rejoice and the seller not mourn’ (verse 12), for the seller will not live to get back what he sold (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
In Judah a king, a temple, priests, prophets and elders still stood, and many people trusted that these guaranteed the city's survival. The poem says the end has come anyway.

Verses 12 and 13 assume a land-owning people. Under the law, family land that was sold was supposed to return to its owner in the year of Jubilee. A seller might grieve losing his field and a buyer rejoice at the gain, but Ezekiel says both reactions are pointless. Conquest will cancel every bargain.

The repetitions, the end, the day, the time, are the point. They hammer home that the delay is over.
passages.later: Amos heard the same word: ‘The end has come for My people Israel’ (Amos 8:2). The law of Jubilee returned family land to its owners (Leviticus 25:10).
passages.asks: The buyer and the seller both thought their deals mattered most. Ask what you are counting on that would not survive a real crisis. And ask what lasts.

passages.t: Silver and gold cannot save them
passages.happening:
The trumpet is blown, but no one goes to war (verse 14). ‘The sword is outside; plague and famine are within’ (verse 15). Survivors flee to the mountains, moaning like doves, and every knee turns to water (verses 16-17). They put on sackcloth and shave their heads (verse 18).

‘They will throw their silver into the streets, and their gold will seem unclean. Their silver and gold cannot save them in the day of the wrath of the LORD’ (verse 19). Their ornaments became idols, and the temple, God's treasured place, will be defiled by foreigners (verses 20-22). The land is full of bloodshed and the city full of violence (verse 23). People will seek a vision from a prophet, instruction from the priests and counsel from the elders, and find none (verse 26). The king will mourn, and God will judge them by their own standards (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Sackcloth, a coarse cloth worn in grief, and shaved heads were common signs of mourning.

Silver and gold were the ancient world's final security. The same metals had been used to make idols, so they became a stumbling block twice over: they fed the people's pride, and they gave shape to their false worship. In the day of disaster they are thrown into the street like rubbish.

Verse 26 names every source of guidance Judah trusted, the prophet, the priest and the elder, and says each will fail. Jeremiah in Jerusalem fought the same false confidence in the same years.
passages.later: Zephaniah said, ‘Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them’ (Zephaniah 1:18). Jeremiah condemned prophets who said ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14).
passages.asks: In the day of trouble the people threw their silver into the streets. Ask what you are trusting for security. And ask what it would mean to hold it more loosely now.
